title: Chip Morning Brief
tldr: AI helps design chips, but three new articles agree: people still check and decide.
AI chips are limited by power, memory cost and heat, not only by transistors.
Nvidia's CEO is back, and export rules keep pushing countries to build their own chips.

cards.head: Three articles, one message: AI helps design chips, people decide

happened.t: Experts from Cadence, Synopsys, universities and AI startups say AI is changing chip design and verification work, and universities are updating curricula.
AI can raise design productivity, but needs scalable data management, good data, IP security and domain understanding.
AI struggles to produce implementable RTL that meets power and performance targets, while high-level synthesis stays strong.
For derivative chip designs, AI helps, but human experts still judge feasibility and cost.

cards.basics: RTL is the code that describes what a chip does, cycle by cycle. High-level synthesis (HLS) turns shorter, C-like code into RTL automatically. A derivative design is a new chip built by changing an older one. The articles say AI is not yet good at producing RTL that meets power and speed goals.
cards.ai: The tools will keep improving, but the part nobody can hand over is judging whether a result is right. Learning RTL, HLS and verification basics keeps you useful next to AI.

cards.head: Power and wiring are becoming design problems for AI chips

happened.t: AI accelerators need high current at low voltage, which moves power delivery to vertical designs with regulators near the processor.
Arteris analysed 1,000 silicon design starts and finds rising system complexity and growing importance of interconnects.
Photonic design must be judged at system level, because parts that each meet spec can behave differently once combined into an optical link.

cards.basics: A chip needs power delivered at a low voltage but a very large current, and big currents lose energy along the way. Putting the voltage regulator close to the processor shortens that path. An interconnect is the wiring network that carries data between blocks inside a chip.
cards.ai: Designers can no longer treat power and wiring as something the package team handles later. Expect them to appear as constraints from the first architecture draft.

cards.head: Denser packages bring heat and radiation problems

happened.t: Amkor's S-SWIFT uses embedded-trace RDL to give die-to-die links more bandwidth for AI, HPC and data-center chips.
Alpha-particle emission is a growing soft-error risk as package density rises.
Diamond Foundry made the first 200mm single-crystal diamond wafer, meant to spread heat from AI chips.
Paper: EOTPR fine-pitch probing isolates die-to-die interconnect defects in chiplet devices.

cards.basics: A chiplet design splits one big chip into several small dies in one package. RDL is the extra wiring layer that connects them. A soft error is a bit that flips because of stray radiation, such as an alpha particle, without any permanent damage. The denser the package, the harder it is to cool, to test and to protect.
cards.ai: Test access, cooling and error protection will probably need planning at the same time as the logic design, not after it.

cards.head: Memory gets expensive, and new kinds of memory are proposed

happened.t: Tesla cut the memory of its AI4.5 chip from 32GB to 24GB because memory costs are rising, moving to LPDDR5X.
Nagare Labs, backed by Pat Gelsinger, is developing Z2RAM, a vertically stacked memory that claims SRAM-like speed with higher density.
SoftBank explored a $1 trillion purchase of SK Hynix but dropped it over financial and regulatory hurdles.

cards.basics: SRAM is very fast memory made from transistors, but it takes a lot of chip area. DRAM is denser but slower and sits outside the chip. LPDDR5X is a low-power kind of DRAM. The memory wall means processors can compute faster than memory can feed them.
cards.ai: When memory is the costly part, architects may be asked to do the same job with less of it. Memory size may become a design target, not a given.

cards.head: Intel Foundry: first outside customer, and a push on yield

happened.t: Intel signed its first external 18A-P customer, according to a weekly roundup.
Intel had signed its first external 18A-P foundry customer and named Microsoft as first customer for EMIB packaging.
Intel Foundry describes joining measurement data, AI analytics and industry standards to raise yield and move toward autonomous production.

cards.basics: A foundry makes chips for other companies. 18A is Intel's newest process name. Yield is the share of chips on a wafer that work. EMIB is Intel's way of linking dies in a package with small silicon bridges.
cards.ai: A second serious foundry option matters to designers because it gives more choice of where to build. It is still early, and one customer is not yet a trend.

cards.head: Nvidia's CEO is reinstated, and the questions remain

happened.t: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO after briefly removing him over alleged ties to a suspected Chinese spy; shares rose 25% premarket.
Nvidia's CEO was first reported to resign after 33 years.
Nvidia's CEO change plus export scrutiny and rare-earth shortages add supply-chain uncertainty, says Sourceability.
An editorial argues that government stakes in firms bias US export-control decisions.

cards.flag: Reports disagree: the first said "resigns", the later one says "briefly removed, then reinstated". The cause is also described differently. The wiki records this as Conflict 4.
cards.ai: For a chip student the story matters mostly as a supply risk. The leader changed back, but the rules around exports did not change.

cards.head: Export controls push countries to build their own chips

happened.t: Alibaba plans to rely mainly on its own T-Head AI chips after 2027 because tighter US export controls threaten supply.
US threats against overseas data-center builders and tighter controls push other governments to diversify AI suppliers.
China's chip exports rose 108% in 2026, about double South Korea's growth.
US export limits on China tightened again, according to a weekly roundup.

cards.basics: An export control is a government rule that limits which chips or tools can be sold to a country. Sovereign AI means a country wants its own AI computing capacity.
cards.ai: If more countries build their own chips, there will be more chip projects and more designer jobs outside the usual few companies. This is a guess, not a result.

cards.head: TSMC says AI demand is strong, and the AI race lifts packaging

happened.t: TSMC sees strong AI chip demand despite market worries, keeps investing in capacity and took a stake in Anthropic.
TSMC's Anthropic stake is 0.03%, bought for US$500 million at the US$83 IPO price.
The AI compute race is lifting demand for GPUs, memory, packaging and data centers.

cards.flag: Earlier reports gave different amounts for TSMC's AI investments. The wiki keeps them as Conflict 1.
cards.ai: The leading foundry betting on AI companies suggests it expects the demand to last. Packaging and memory keep appearing next to GPUs, so those fields are likely to stay busy.

take: AI helps with chip design but does not replace the checking, so fundamentals (RTL, verification) still matter.
Power, memory and heat are now design constraints that appear from the start of a project.
Export rules keep reshaping who builds chips, so supply and policy news is worth a glance.
